implementation_notes: Moq builds the double from an interface or a class with virtual members using LINQ expression trees and Castle DynamicProxy, so expectations are ordinary lambdas: Setup(w => w.HasInventory("Talisker", 50)).Returns(true) programmes behaviour, Verify(...) checks the calls, and It/Times matchers refine arguments and cardinality. The hand-written double survives only where a type cannot be intercepted (sealed or final types, non-virtual members) or where dynamic proxies are banned by policy.
pitfalls: The default MockBehavior.Loose returns default values for unstubbed members, so a forgotten Setup lets a test pass against null or zero; MockBehavior.Strict turns that silence into a failure.
Only virtual members are intercepted: a non-virtual or sealed member executes the real code while the test believes it is verifying a double.
Mocking third-party types with Moq is possible but still unwise - wrap the dependency in an interface you own so the mock encodes your contract, not the library's.

variants.name: NSubstitute substitute (Arrange-Act-Assert)
variants.implementation_notes: NSubstitute obtains the double from Substitute.For<T>() and keeps configuration and verification close to natural language: .Returns(...) programmes behaviour, .Received()/.DidNotReceive() with Arg.Any/Arg.Is matchers check the calls that must or must not have happened, and Raise.Event() raises collaborator events. It also intercepts interfaces and virtual members through dynamic proxies; choose it when the team prefers post-hoc Received() checks over Moq's Setup/Verify pair.
pitfalls: Received() checks run after the exercise phase, so a deviating call is reported at the end of the test rather than when it happened; use Received.InOrder when sequence matters.
A substitute left unconfigured returns default substitutes rather than failing, so unstubbed paths can pass silently - configure the members the requirement exercises.
